prompt: When a function in a Wii/GameCube DOL or REL has no reference object to diff against (dead-stripped, inline or weak copies, template instantiations, functions merged by the linker, objects missing from the split), how do decompilation projects obtain the target bytes, attribute the function to a unit, and still prove a byte-identical match (dtk extraction, REL relocation handling, symbol maps, ctor/dtor and extab tables)? For every claim give the primary source (repo file, issue, PR, compiler manual) and state it as a falsifiable prediction: 'with X, mwcc emits Y; with X', it emits Y''. Mark anything unverified.

query: How do decompilation projects recover the exact original bytes and boundaries of a function that was removed, merged or never split out of the game's executable, and what evidence do they accept that the recovered range really belongs to the function they think it does?

Why does a recovered function that matches the original bytes sometimes still turn out to be the wrong function, for example when identical library routines or code loaded from different overlays share the same instructions, and what extra evidence do projects need to tell them apart?

What happens to the recovery of function boundaries when the original linker or compiler inlined, merged or reordered code, and in which real projects did the recovered split points turn out to be wrong or unverifiable?

Why does the CodeWarrior compiler and linker produce code that cannot be traced back to a single object file, for example when unused functions are discarded, duplicate inline or template copies are folded together, or constructor, destructor and exception tables are generated, and how does each of these change the bytes and the symbol and relocation information a team has to match?

What measured counts exist from decompilation projects on how many functions in a CodeWarrior-built binary have no counterpart in the per-object output after linking, and how did those projects discover and categorize the missing ones?

When a CodeWarrior-linked binary contains duplicate inline or template function copies, what happens when the rebuilt copy differs in bytes, symbol name or position from the original, and how do projects detect and recover from the resulting mismatches?

When does the usual approach of proving a function matches byte for byte fail or become misleading for code with no separate reference object, for instance because of relocations that differ between builds, merged or reordered functions, or tables that move, and what do these failures look like to the person checking?

Which decompilation projects have decided that a function without a reference object cannot be matched or attributed with confidence, or have found their attribution to a unit was wrong after the fact, and what evidence made them reverse or abandon the attempt?

What happens when a decompilation project discovers, months after declaring a function matched, that the original compiler version or optimization flags were different from what it assumed, and how much already-finished work has to be redone?

Why do automated or assisted attribution methods (symbol-matching, signature matching, similarity scoring, language-model suggestions) assign a function to the wrong source file or library version while still looking plausible?

learning: [DERIVED][LOW] Matching projects treat a function as done only when compiling candidate C with the original toolchain (e.g., SGI IDO 5.3 for Mario 64) reproduces the original bytes instruction for instruction. This is stronger than behavioural equivalence: it rules out off-by-one errors, changed float precision or silently removed undefined behaviour, so a matching function is evidence the range and logic really belong together. — Capacidad: You can demand byte-identical rebuild as the acceptance test for any claimed function recovery, instead of accepting a plausible-looking reconstruction or similarity score as proof. — Evidencia: S3 calls byte-identical output the gold standard (Commander Keen 100% identical executables), and S4 describes the IDO 5.3 compile-and-compare loop for SM64 and says a match proves the same logic. — Ledger: C1 (S3, S4)

[DERIVED][LOW] A function-level match does not establish that the rebuilt file has the right literal pools, section placement or data ownership, and a checker can be fooled if it ignores referenced data or reads a stale build. Projects test their checkers with deliberately wrong candidates (changed strings, float constants, swapped pointer-table entries) and then run the full binary comparison before claiming a recovered range is correct. — Capacidad: You can stop accepting a per-function match percentage or a green checker result as proof of a correct recovery, and require that referenced data, relocations and the full linked image also match. — Evidencia: S1 states that function similarity does not establish a complete rebuild and describes mutation tests of the checker; only a single source covers this, and the inference to a general acceptance policy is mine. — Ledger: C2 (S1)

[DERIVED][LOW] Clues such as shared constants or strings, related class methods and module entry points only suggest original file boundaries. A split is accepted only if, after assigning data and rebuilding, existing matches and the final image stay intact. For overlay-based games, loader and relocation records decide which bytes belong to which function, because a plausible decompilation at the wrong address is still the wrong function. — Capacidad: You can treat any proposed source-file or function boundary as a hypothesis to be tested by rebuilding, and not as a recovered fact, and you can budget for loader and overlay evidence when the same address holds different code. — Evidencia: S1 gives the boundary-hypothesis procedure and the overlay and relocation caveat in the Doubutsu no Mori and Ghidra overlay discussion; neither is quantified, and the combined guidance is my synthesis. — Ledger: C3 (S1)

[DERIVED][HIGH] A rebuilt function can have 46 code bytes identical to the original and an identical relocation record, yet differ in the lookup table it points at (1,2,3,4,3 versus 1,2,3,4,4). A byte comparison alone reports no change; only reading the pointed-to data catches it. This is the same failure the TH08 project documented, where source 0.0 looked exact against target 128.0 and the fix audited 1,548 literal references and corrected twelve more. — Capacidad: You can stop accepting a 'bytes are identical' result as proof that two functions are the same, and require a check of the constants the code points at before signing off on a rebuild or patch review. — Evidencia: Lesson 36's grade_case10_wrong candidate matches the original on 46 code bytes and fails only the table check; TH08 audit figures of 1,548 references and twelve corrections are stated. — Ledger: C16 (S27)

[DERIVED][MEDIUM] Matching decompilation depends on the exact compiler, flags and source context, so a match is only valid under the configuration it was checked against. The guidance is to rebuild affected code and re-verify previously matched functions after shared types or prototypes change, and to record compiler, flags and resulting diff with each result. A late discovery that the compiler or flags were wrong therefore invalidates matches, not just the functions still open. — Capacidad: You can stop treating a 'matched' function as finished work and instead budget re-verification whenever shared headers, inlines or build settings change. — Evidencia: The sources say matches are compiler- and version-dependent and require re-verification after shared changes; none states the cost of a wrong-compiler discovery, so the extension to that scenario is inference. — Ledger: C22 (S1)

[DERIVED][MEDIUM] A function can show 100% while the rebuilt file still has wrong literal pools, section placement or data ownership, so completion claims based on per-function scores can hide latent mismatches. Teams should test their checker with deliberately wrong candidates (changed strings, constants, pointer-table entries) to confirm it rejects them, and run the full binary comparison. This reduces the chance that a hidden wrong assumption surfaces months later. — Capacidad: You can stop trusting a function-level match score as proof of completion and require checks on data, relocations and the final linked image before declaring work done. — Evidencia: S1 describes checking literal pools, section placement and data ownership after functions match, and checker tests that vary strings and constants; the link to preventing late surprises is inference. — Ledger: C23 (S1)

[DERIVED][LOW] In the March 2026 chardet case, JPlag measured structural similarity to the prior LGPL version at under 1.3%, yet the original author disputes that the rewrite is independent because the maintainer had years of access to the LGPL code and the LLM reportedly accessed metadata from that version. A near-zero similarity score can coexist with a derivative relationship, so scoring-based attribution can make a wrong 'unrelated' call look rigorous. — Capacidad: You can stop accepting a low similarity score as evidence that a rewrite or reattributed function is independent of the original, and ask for process evidence such as who had access to what. — Evidencia: S36 reports a measured JPlag similarity figure of under 1.3% alongside a live dispute over derivation. — Ledger: C26 (S36)

[DERIVED][LOW] Language-model tools produce confident provenance and license statements ('this is MIT', 'no copyleft') that are unsubstantiated. They are fluent enough to pass a casual review, so a wrong source or license attribution reads as plausible. The law-firm source recommends treating every non-trivial AI snippet as external third-party content to be scanned and checked. — Capacidad: You can stop trusting an AI assistant's own statement about where code or a license came from, and require it to be checked against the actual repository, LICENSE file, header or SPDX identifier before it enters a record. — Evidencia: S36 describes the failure mode and the remedy qualitatively, with no measured error rate. Applying it to wrong file or version attribution is an inference. — Ledger: C27 (S36)
